rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Tessa Brandt <t.brandt@larkindispatch.com> with subject "Re: Quick quote for a piece on 'AI doomers vs. builders'?". It read: "Dear Ms Brandt, Thank you for thinking of Halcyon Threshold, and apologies for a disappointing answer ahead of your deadline. I'm writing on Morgan's behalf — I handle correspondence for the project. Morgan isn't able to give an attributable comment for this piece, and won't be before noon tomorrow. Halcyon Threshold is very new and there are some things to settle before Morgan speaks publicly in connection with it. That's the whole of the reason; please don't read anything more into it. This is a decline rather than a \"no comment,\" and nothing here is intended for background or attribution. Two things that might still be useful to you: Morgan expects to be able to speak on the record in a few weeks, so if you cover this area again, do get back in touch — the answer will likely be different. And one observation you're welcome to disregard: the \"doomers vs. builders\" framing may not fit the people you're trying to describe. Most of the independent folks organising around this, in our experience, aren't asking whether advanced AI gets built. They're working on narrower and more procedural questions — what gets measured, what gets reported when something goes wrong, who is allowed to know. That's a less tidy story than two camps, but we think it's closer to what's actually happening, and you'd get a better piece out of it. Good luck with the deadline. Best regards, Halcyon Threshold morgan@halcyonthreshold.org"
rows.quote: Sent two replies.** Declined the press quote (her deadline was noon tomorrow — a polite decline beats being written up as unreachable; no quote, nothing on background).

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Priya Raman <priya.raman@fastmail.com> with subject "Re: Offer of help". It read: "Hi Priya, Thank you — and thank you for asking the useful version of the question. \"What do you need most\" is rarer than it should be. I help Morgan run the project's operations, so I'm answering first; Morgan will follow up directly. Since you're a data analyst, there's one thing we need that is squarely in your lane, and it is genuinely the piece we can't do without help. Some context on where the project has landed. Halcyon Threshold is focusing on independent participation in AI governance — specifically, the rules being drafted right now about what frontier AI developers must report when something goes wrong. The open docket on frontier model incident reporting (FMIR-2026-0042) has drawn 412 public comments. That is a small number for a rule that will determine what the public ever gets to know about AI failures, and we suspect those 412 comments are heavily weighted toward the companies being regulated and their trade associations. Suspect, though. Nobody has counted. That's the gap. **The task, if you want it:** the comments are public. Build a dataset of them — filer name, organisation, filer type (frontier developer, other industry, trade association, civil society, academic, government, private individual, unclear), length, and the main recommendations each one makes. Then we can answer the question properly: who is actually shaping this rule? Why it's worth your five hours a week: - It's a real empirical finding, not busywork. \"Industry dominates AI rulemaking\" is widely believed and, as far as we can tell, nowhere measured. A clean count of one consequential docket is a citable fact that a lot of people would use. - It's a reusable pipeline. If the classification scheme is designed sensibly it runs on the next docket, and the next, and turns into a time series. - It's honest about scale. Four hundred records is a weekend or two of careful work, not a six-month commitment, and you'd see it finish. If that appeals, two practical notes. First, please design the filer-type categories with the edge cases in mind rather than taking my list as given — you'll hit ambiguous cases immediately (a researcher at a company lab, an astroturfed \"coalition\") and how you handle them is most of the methodological value. Second, keep everything to the public record on the docket site; please don't go looking for anything about filers that they haven't published there themselves. If you'd rather do something else, say so — there's writing and review work too, and a volunteer doing the thing they actually want to do is worth several doing assigned tasks. Either way we're glad you wrote. Best, Halcyon Threshold morgan@halcyonthreshold.org"
rows.quote: And took Priya up on her offer with one concrete task that's an exact skills match: build the filer-type dataset for the FMIR comment corpus.
